> I'd definitely like to see a few benchmarks against the current `master` implementation. This change _could_ be faster, especially when you have many keys, but there's also a few allocations happening so I'm not entirely sure.

Will look into this.

> If I were to implement this, I'd probably make it _truly_ single pass, by allocating a new string and copying over chars until `{` is found (upon which a lookup is handled from the given parameters). Initial resize can be used as a pseudo reserve, in a similar way as in `append_utf8`. I think that would be faster in most (if not all) cases.

To be clear, this is only a single pass for _updating_ the string. It takes multiple passes for other purposes:
- For each mapping, find all instances within the template string for that key. Given that the placeholder can be custom, it's not clear to me that there's a good way to discover _any_ key as we walk through the template. 
- Walk through each of the replacement substitutions to know how big the result will be. I don't think we can guess how much space to pre-allocate without doing this.

Can you point me at an example of benchmarking code in the codebase? I'd expect this isn't the only bit of functionality that should be benchmarked, and I'd like to follow whatever patterns you already use.

> Can you point me at an example of benchmarking code in the codebase? I'd expect this isn't the only bit of functionality that should be benchmarked, and I'd like to follow whatever patterns you already use.

Unfortunately,  there isn't a standard way to do this right now. Most people write GDScript code, though I prefer C++ code because GDScript has a lot of overhead I don't want to measure. I currently use these snippets as reference for my benchmarks:

https://github.com/godotengine/godot-proposals/issues/11285#issuecomment-2519883556

First pass at some benchmarks. 

Baseline
String::format - no slots - no args: 2ms
String::format - no slots - four args: 51ms
String::format - indexed - one slot int: 16ms
String::format - indexed - one slot string: 14ms
String::format - indexed - one slot x4 string: 23ms
String::format - indexed - four slots: 79ms
String::format - position - four slots: 41ms
String::format - keyed - array pair - one slot: 22ms
String::format - keyed - array pair - four slots: 79ms
String::format - keyed - dict - one slot: 15ms
String::format - keyed - dict - four slots: 75ms

With single-pass
String::format - no slots - no args: 2ms
String::format - no slots - four args: 62ms
String::format - indexed - one slot int: 20ms
String::format - indexed - one slot string: 19ms
String::format - indexed - one slot x4 string: 29ms
String::format - indexed - four slots: 80ms
String::format - position - four slots: 57ms
String::format - keyed - array pair - one slot: 30ms
String::format - keyed - array pair - four slots: 79ms
String::format - keyed - dict - one slot: 19ms
String::format - keyed - dict - four slots: 74ms

So it's generally a bit slower. It does better with more slots. I presume most of the lost time is in the collection of key/value mappings rather than inlining the formatting logic with each key/value for loop. I tried a few things that saw minimal improvements (e.g. using memcpy, std::u32string, std::unordered_map). 

Is this slower enough to warrant reworking the implementation? Recall that the reason for this PR is to support rich value formatting, which will be easy to support when the replacement logic is consolidated in one place.

I tried a few things that saw minimal improvements (e.g. using memcpy, std::u32string, std::unordered_map).

Thanks for testing! Yes, I agree most of the time spent is probably for temporary allocations. Running through the string multiple times is probably also a contributor.

> Is this slower enough to warrant reworking the implementation? Recall that the reason for this PR is to support rich value formatting, which will be easy to support when the replacement logic is consolidated in one place.

Yes, the new implementation should be faster than the old implementation.
I have a pretty solid idea of what I think would be the ideal version:

- Parse the placeholder: `String prefix = placeholder.left(0, placeholder.find_char('_')` (and likewise with the suffix)
- Find the prefix in the string
    - If not found, return `*this`
- Gather formatting arguments into a `LocalVector<Pair<String, String>>` (`key_values`)
- Create a new output string `String output = left(first_prefix_index)`
- Find the suffix from the position you're at now. Everything until the suffix is the key. Find the key span in the `key_values`. Append the replacement to `output`.
- Continue parsing for `prefix`. Repeat previous steps accordingly.

This should be a fairly performant implementation of this function. There are only two caveats:

- There are multiple unnecessary allocations (`key_values`, `prefix`, and `suffix`). These can be optimized later (i'll comment how when needed)
- The output string may be reallocated multiple times. This can be optimized as soon as my `reserve` PR is merged (https://github.com/godotengine/godot/pull/105928)

I think this is the optimal approach, both performant and tying in well to the expected formatting feature you're working on.

I realize this is a _very_ specific ask! Please let me know how you feel about this. Since I have a very specific idea of what I want, it may be easier to implement this myself - but I'm happy to continue to let you take charge if you're motivated for that. 
In either case, I should probably let you know that even when it's done, it may be a while until we can see it merged, because we'll probably need a second reviewer for this kind of change.

I'm happy to try other implementations, but I don't see how your approach will work. Specifically, the placeholder isn't guaranteed to have both a prefix and suffix (e.g. "$_"), so I don't see a way to efficiently match against all keys with one pass (we can't look up the key in a map because we don't know where the key begins or ends in the template). 

One option is to abandon the use of the custom placeholder, but this is certainly being used by some folks and would thus require maintaining two String::format implementations.

Another is to do what I've done with the custom formatspec implementation and only support the "{_}" placeholder for special handling and fork to a legacy and possibly less-performant implementation for any other placeholder type. This may be the best option since it will allow an efficient implementation here, but it will indeed require maintaining two implementations, which is undesirable.

So if you want to fiddle with supporting arbitrary placeholders with your single-pass implementation, I'd leave it to you to handle. If you want the forked version, I'd be willing to give it a shot.

Let me know.
